- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

data.answer: The neural network is better than just guessing the median because it's trained on more data and has more accurate weights.
data.context:

On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The neural network is better than just guessing the median because it uses more accurate and detailed data. The 4 inputs and 16 hidden layers allow it to capture more information and make more accurate predictions.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

data.context:

On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

No. This is a class exhibit built on synthetic data, not staffing, medical or business advice.

[2] What visitors can discover
- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

[3] Limitations
- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.
- The model only knows hours 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 staff, and 0 to 20 patients in the queue. It should not be used outside those ranges.
- We have not tested the model on any other dataset or in any real clinic, so we have no results for how well it would work there.
- The model finds patterns in the data; it does not prove what causes waits. It is not medical, staffing or business advice.
- 8% of test visits were off by more than 10 minutes.

- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.

Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):

- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).

- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The neural network is better than just guessing the median because it is trained on more data and has more layers.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: A: Yes, the neural network is better than just guessing the median.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The neural network is better than just guessing the median because it is trained on more data and has more layers to learn.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

[4] Not covered by this guide

- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

data.q: How did your model compare with the baseline?
data.answer: A: The model's error was 90% lower than the baseline.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).

- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: Yes. The neural network's error was 90% lower than the median baseline.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.context:
[1] Quick answer — Should a real clinic use this to decide staffing?
No. This is a class exhibit built on synthetic data, not staffing, medical or business advice.

[2] What visitors can discover
- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

[3] Limitations
- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.
- The model only knows hours 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 staff, and 0 to 20 patients in the queue. It should not be used outside those ranges.
- We have not tested the model on any other dataset or in any real clinic, so we have no results for how well it would work there.
- The model finds patterns in the data; it does not prove what causes waits. It is not medical, staffing or business advice.
- 8% of test visits were off by more than 10 minutes.

[4] Not covered by this guide
This guide does not cover real clinics or hospitals, costs, staffing policy, medical questions, other datasets, or details of how the data was simulated beyond what is written here.

data.q: How did your model compare with the baseline?
data.answer: The guide doesn't cover that. This exhibit is built on synthetic data and is not staffing advice.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

[3] Limitations
- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.
- The model only knows hours 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 staff, and 0 to 20 patients in the queue. It should not be used outside those ranges.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The guide doesn't cover that. This exhibit is built on synthetic data and is not a predictive model.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.

- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer:
Yes, the neural network is better than just guessing the median.  
A: The neural network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline.  
A: The neural network predicts wait times more accurately than a simple median guess.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.

[2] What visitors can discover
- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

[3] Limitations
- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.
- The model only knows hours 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 staff, and 0 to 20 patients in the queue. It should not be used outside those ranges.
- We have not tested the model on any other dataset or in any real clinic, so we have no results for how well it would work there.
- The model finds patterns in the data; it does not prove what causes waits. It is not medical, staffing or business advice.
- 8% of test visits were off by more than 10 minutes.

data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.q: Should we add more nurses at our clinic?
data.answer: The guide doesn't cover that. This exhibit is built on synthetic data and is not staffing advice.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — Should a real clinic use this to decide staffing?
No. This is a class exhibit built on synthetic data, not staffing, medical or business advice.

[2] What visitors can discover
- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

[3] Limitations
- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.
- The model only knows hours 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 staff, and 0 to 20 patients in the queue. It should not be used outside those ranges.
- We have not tested the model on any other dataset or in any real clinic, so we have no results for how well it would work there.
- The model finds patterns in the data; it does not prove what causes waits. It is not medical, staffing or business advice.
- 8% of test visits were off by more than 10 minutes.

[4] Not covered by this guide
This guide does not cover real clinics or hospitals, costs, staffing policy, medical questions, other datasets, or details of how the data was simulated beyond what is written here.

data.q: How did your model compare with the baseline?
data.answer: The model compared with the baseline by having a 90% lower error.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

[2] Quick answer — Should a real clinic use this to decide staffing?
No. This is a class exhibit built on synthetic data, not staffing, medical or business advice.

[3] Where the data came from
The data is the file clinic-wait-times.csv from the course website (https://snsie.github.io/neural-networks/data/clinic-wait-times.csv). It contains 2,000 simulated clinic visits. The data is synthetic (made up): it does not describe any real clinic, hospital or patient. Each visit records the hour (8 am to 5 pm), the weekday (Monday to Friday), the staff on shift (1 to 5), the patients already in the queue (0 to 20), and the wait in minutes (0 to 324).
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The neural network's error was 90% lower than the median baseline, indicating it is better than just guessing the median.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.

data.answer: The guide doesn't cover that. This exhibit is built on synthetic data and is not staffing advice.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — Should a real clinic use this to decide staffing?
No. This is a class exhibit built on synthetic data, not staffing, medical or business advice.

[2] What visitors can discover
- Staffing has diminishing returns. With 12 patients waiting on Monday at 9 am, the network predicts 198 minutes with 1 staff, 100 with 2, 76 with 3, 58 with 4 and 51 with 5. The 2nd staff member saves about 98 minutes; the 5th saves about 7.
- Each patient in the queue adds roughly 15 minutes, divided by the number of staff on shift.
- Peak hours (9 am–10 am and 4 pm–5 pm) run longer, and Mondays run about 5% longer than other weekdays.

[3] Limitations
- The data is synthetic, so the results say nothing about any real clinic.
- The model only knows hours 8 am to 5 pm, Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 staff, and 0 to 20 patients in the queue. It should not be used outside those ranges.
- We have not tested the model on any other dataset or in any real clinic, so we have no results for how well it would work there.
- The model finds patterns in the data; it does not prove what causes waits. It is not medical, staffing or business advice.
- 8% of test visits were off by more than 10 minutes.

[4] Not covered by this guide
This guide does not cover real clinics or hospitals, costs, staffing policy, medical questions, other datasets, or details of how the data was simulated beyond what is written here.
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The guide doesn't cover that. The neural network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline, which is 46.14 minutes.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.

data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.

data.q: Is the neural network better than just guessing the median?
data.answer: The guide doesn't cover that. This exhibit is built on synthetic data and is not staffing advice. The model's error was 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.
data.context:
[1] Quick answer — How did the model compare with the baseline?
On the 300 held-out test visits, the neural network's average error was 4.49 minutes. The median baseline, which always predicts 59.5 minutes, had an average error of 46.14 minutes. The network's error was 90% lower.

[2] What the model sees and predicts
- Inputs: hour, weekday, staff on shift, and patients in the queue.
- Output: the predicted wait in minutes.
- Model: a small neural network (a multilayer perceptron). The 4 inputs are encoded as 17 numbers (hour and weekday one-hot, staff and queue standardized), followed by two hidden layers of 16 and 8 ReLU neurons and one output. It has 433 weights in total.
- It was trained in Python with PyTorch, exported to ONNX, and runs in the visitor's browser with ONNX Runtime Web.

[3] Results on the test set
Mean absolute error (the average size of a miss; lower is better):
- Neural network: 4.49 minutes (95% interval 4.1 to 4.9).
- Median baseline, which always predicts the training median of 59.5 minutes: 46.14 minutes.
- Linear regression on the same inputs: 26.11 minutes.
- Queue-divided-by-staff formula: 5.60 minutes.

The network's error is 90% lower than the median baseline. 92% of test visits were predicted within 10 minutes of the actual wait, and R² was 0.994.
Monday at 9 am, 2 staff on shift, 12 patients in the queue. The network predicts a wait of 100 minutes. With one more staff member, the network predicts 76 minutes.
